[← Back to Bioinformatics for "Dumb Me"](index.qmd)

Building a personal website may sound complicated if you have never worked with web development before. Fortunately, you do not need to know much HTML, CSS, or JavaScript to get started.

One relatively simple approach is to use **Quarto + GitHub + GitHub Pages**.

This is also how I built this website.

The basic idea is:

> **Write → Quarto → Git → GitHub → GitHub Pages**

More specifically:

```text
Write .qmd files
        ↓
Quarto builds the website
        ↓
Git tracks your changes
        ↓
GitHub stores your project
        ↓
GitHub Pages publishes your website
```

This guide explains the whole process from the beginning, using my website as an example.

---

## 1. What do you need?

There are five main components:

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Quarto** | Converts `.qmd` files into webpages |
| **VS Code** | A convenient editor for writing and managing the project |
| **Git** | Tracks changes to your files |
| **GitHub** | Stores your project online |
| **GitHub Pages** | Hosts your public website |

You do not need to understand all of them before starting.

In fact, building a website is a good way to learn how these tools work together.

### Check Quarto

Open your terminal and run:

```bash
quarto --version
```

### Check Git

```bash
git --version
```

If both commands return version numbers, you are ready to continue.

---

## 2. Create a Quarto website

Choose a name for your project.

For a GitHub Pages personal website, a useful convention is:

```text
YOUR-USERNAME.github.io
```

Create the project:

```bash
quarto create project website YOUR-USERNAME.github.io
```

Then enter the project:

```bash
cd YOUR-USERNAME.github.io
```

### My example

My GitHub username is:

```text
Trieu-Le1211
```

So my project is:

```bash
quarto create project website Trieu-Le1211.github.io
```

and the project directory is:

```text
Trieu-Le1211.github.io/
```

---

## 3. Understand `_quarto.yml`

One of the most important files in a Quarto website is:

```text
_quarto.yml
```

Think of this as the **configuration file for the whole website**.

It can control:

- Website title
- Navigation bar
- Theme
- CSS
- Page structure
- Search
- Social links
- Other site-wide settings

A simple example is:

```yaml
project:
  type: website

website:
  title: "Your Name"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: about.qmd
        text: About
      - href: publications.qmd
        text: Publications
      - href: blog/index.qmd
        text: Blog

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    css: styles.css
    toc: true
```

### My example

My website has sections for my academic background, publications, bioinformatics notes, and personal writing:

```yaml
project:
  type: website

website:
  title: "Trieu Le"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: about.qmd
        text: About Me
      - href: publications.qmd
        text: Publications
      - href: bioinformatics/index.qmd
        text: Bioinformatics for Dummies
      - href: thoughts/index.qmd
        text: Thoughts

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    css: styles.css
    toc: true
```

Notice that the navigation links point to `.qmd` files.

Quarto will convert them into the appropriate webpage links when the website is rendered.

---

## 4. Organise your website

A small personal website might look like this:

```text
YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/
│
├── _quarto.yml
├── index.qmd
├── about.qmd
├── publications.qmd
├── styles.css
│
├── images/
│
└── blog/
    ├── index.qmd
    ├── article-1.qmd
    └── article-2.qmd
```

My website has a similar structure:

```text
Trieu-Le1211.github.io/
│
├── _quarto.yml
├── index.qmd
├── about.qmd
├── publications.qmd
├── styles.css
│
├── images/
│
├── bioinformatics/
│   ├── index.qmd
│   └── bayesian-statistics.qmd
│
└── thoughts/
    ├── index.qmd
    ├── just-start-writing.qmd
    └── science-through-the-lens-of-investing.qmd
```

The important idea is:

> **One `.qmd` file can become one webpage.**

For example:

```text
about.qmd
```

becomes:

```text
about.html
```

when Quarto renders the website.

---

## 5. Write your first `.qmd` page

Quarto documents use a combination of **YAML** and **Markdown**.

For example, create:

```text
about.qmd
```

and write:

```markdown
---
title: "About Me"
toc: false
---

## Hello, I'm Your Name

I am a researcher interested in **your research interests here**.

## Research interests

- Research area 1
- Research area 2
- Research area 3
- Research area 4
```

The part between:

```text
---
...
---
```

is the **YAML metadata**.

For example:

```yaml
title: "About Me"
toc: false
```

The rest is Markdown.

Some basic Markdown syntax:

```markdown
# Main heading

## Subheading

### Smaller heading

**bold**

*italic*

- Item 1
- Item 2
- Item 3

[Link text](https://example.com)
```

You therefore do not need to write most of your website in HTML.

---

## 6. Create a blog

One of the main reasons I wanted a personal website was to have somewhere to write.

A useful way to organise a blog is to create a directory:

```text
blog/
```

Inside it:

```text
blog/
├── index.qmd
├── article-1.qmd
├── article-2.qmd
└── article-3.qmd
```

Each article gets its own `.qmd` file.

For example:

```text
blog/my-first-article.qmd
```

with:

```yaml
---
title: "My First Article"
subtitle: "What this article is about"
date: 2026-09-27
author: "Your Name"
categories:
  - Research
  - Reflections
toc: false
---
```

Then write the article below the YAML header.

### My example

I have a section called:

```text
thoughts/
```

where I write about research, my PhD, scientific writing, conferences, and other things I find interesting.

For example:

```text
thoughts/just-start-writing.qmd
```

starts with:

```yaml
---
title: "Just Start Writing"
subtitle: "You have a report or thesis to write—what are you waiting for?"
date: 2026-09-26
categories:
  - Research
  - Writing
author: "Trieu Le"
toc: false
---
```

The rest of the file contains the article.

---

## 7. Automatically list your articles

You do not have to manually update your blog homepage every time you write something.

Quarto can automatically find your articles and create a listing.

For example, `blog/index.qmd` can contain:

```yaml
---
title: "Blog"
description: "My writing about research, science, and other things."

listing:
  contents:
    - "*.qmd"
    - "!index.qmd"
  sort: "date desc"
  type: default
  fields:
    - title
    - subtitle
    - date
    - categories

page-layout: full
toc: false
---
```

Now imagine you have:

```text
blog/
├── index.qmd
├── article-a.qmd
├── article-b.qmd
└── article-c.qmd
```

Quarto will automatically list:

```text
article-a
article-b
article-c
```

on the Blog page.

If you add:

```text
article-d.qmd
```

you do not need to manually add it to `index.qmd`.

Render the website again and Quarto will find it.

### My example

I use this system for two sections:

```text
thoughts/
```

and:

```text
bioinformatics/
```

This allows me to keep personal reflections and technical bioinformatics notes separate while using the same underlying system.

---

## 8. Add images

Create an image directory:

```text
images/
```

For example:

```text
images/
├── profile.jpg
├── conference-timeline.png
└── writing-science.jpg
```

You can insert an image into a `.qmd` document using:

```markdown
![Description of the image](images/example.png)
```

You can control its width and alignment:

```markdown
![Description of the image](images/example.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}
```

### My example

In one of my posts, I include a picture of a book using:

```markdown
!["Writing Science" by Joshua Schimel](images/writing_science.jpg){fig-align="center" width="40%"}
```

Quarto places the image exactly where I put that line in the article.

### A small lesson I learned

Try to use simple filenames:

```text
writing-science.jpg
conference-timeline.png
my-first-conference.jpg
```

rather than:

```text
My First Conference FINAL version 2.JPG
```

Lowercase filenames without spaces are easier to manage and reduce the risk of path problems when publishing online.

---

## 9. Customise the appearance with CSS

Quarto controls the content and structure of the website, while CSS can be used to change its appearance.

Create:

```text
styles.css
```

and tell Quarto to use it in `_quarto.yml`:

```yaml
format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    css: styles.css
```

For example:

```css
img {
  border-radius: 8px;
}
```

or:

```css
.photo-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  gap: 15px;
}

.photo-grid img {
  width: 100%;
  height: auto;
}
```

This can be used to create a three-column photo gallery.

You do not need much CSS when you first build the website. Start with one of Quarto's themes and customise things gradually.

---

## 10. Render the website

Once you have written your pages, run:

```bash
quarto render
```

Quarto reads the source files and generates the website.

The rendered website is normally placed in:

```text
_site/
```

For example:

```text
_site/
├── index.html
├── about.html
├── publications.html
├── blog/
└── images/
```

The relationship is:

```text
index.qmd  → index.html
about.qmd  → about.html
```

So remember:

> **Edit the `.qmd` files, not the generated `.html` files.**

---

## 11. Preview the website locally

Before publishing the website, check how it looks on your own computer.

Quarto normally provides:

```bash
quarto preview
```

This renders the website and starts a local preview.

Alternatively, after running:

```bash
quarto render
```

you can serve `_site/` using Python:

```bash
python3 -m http.server 8000 --directory _site
```

Then open:

```text
http://localhost:8000
```

in your browser.

A simple development workflow is therefore:

```text
Edit
  ↓
Save
  ↓
quarto render
  ↓
Check locally
  ↓
Edit again
```

Repeat until you are happy with the result.

---

## 12. Start tracking the project with Git

Once the website is working locally, initialise Git.

Go to your project:

```bash
cd path/to/YOUR-USERNAME.github.io
```

Then:

```bash
git init
```

Rename the main branch:

```bash
git branch -M main
```

Add your files:

```bash
git add .
```

Create your first commit:

```bash
git commit -m "Initial website"
```

A **commit** is essentially a saved checkpoint in the history of your project.

---

## 13. Configure your Git identity

The first time you use Git, you may see:

```text
Author identity unknown
```

If so, configure your name:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
```

and email:

```bash
git config --global user.email "your-email@example.com"
```

Check them:

```bash
git config --global user.name
git config --global user.email
```

Then try committing again.

---

## 14. Create a GitHub repository

Next, create a GitHub repository.

For a personal GitHub Pages user site, name the repository:

```text
YOUR-USERNAME.github.io
```

For example, if your GitHub username is:

```text
alice
```

the repository would be:

```text
alice.github.io
```

and the website can be published at:

```text
https://alice.github.io
```

### My example

My username is:

```text
Trieu-Le1211
```

so my repository is:

```text
Trieu-Le1211.github.io
```

and my website is:

```text
https://Trieu-Le1211.github.io
```

---

## 15. Connect the local project to GitHub

Git knows about the files on your computer, but it does not yet know where the GitHub repository is.

Connect them with:

```bash
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/YOUR-USERNAME.github.io.git
```

Check:

```bash
git remote -v
```

You should see something like:

```text
origin  https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/YOUR-USERNAME.github.io.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/YOUR-USERNAME.github.io.git (push)
```

Then push the source files:

```bash
git push -u origin main
```

GitHub does not accept your normal GitHub account password for Git operations over HTTPS. Use a supported authentication method, such as GitHub authentication through your editor, a credential manager, or a personal access token.

---

## 16. Understand repository vs website

This distinction confused me initially, but it is actually quite simple.

Your **GitHub repository** contains things such as:

```text
index.qmd
about.qmd
_quarto.yml
styles.css
images/
```

It is the source of your website and contains the Git history.

Your **GitHub Pages website** contains what visitors see in their browser.

Conceptually:

```text
SOURCE

.qmd
.yml
.css
images
   ↓
 Quarto
   ↓
RENDERED WEBSITE

.html
CSS
images
```

Then GitHub Pages makes the rendered website available on the internet.

So:

> **GitHub repository = project**

> **GitHub Pages = public website**

---

## 17. Publish the website

Once the website works locally, publish it with:

```bash
quarto publish gh-pages
```

Quarto creates or updates a Git branch called:

```text
gh-pages
```

Then open your GitHub repository and go to:

```text
Settings
→ Pages
```

Choose:

```text
Source:
Deploy from a branch

Branch:
gh-pages

Folder:
/ (root)
```

GitHub Pages will then publish the rendered website.

For a user website, the address will normally be:

```text
https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io
```

### My example

Mine is:

```text
https://Trieu-Le1211.github.io
```

---

## 18. The normal workflow after setup

The long setup above only needs to be done once.

After that, maintaining the website is much simpler.

Imagine you create:

```text
blog/my-new-article.qmd
```

Write your article and then render:

```bash
quarto render
```

Check the website locally.

When you are happy with it:

```bash
git add .
```

Commit the changes:

```bash
git commit -m "Add new article"
```

Push the source files to GitHub:

```bash
git push
```

Then publish the updated website:

```bash
quarto publish gh-pages
```

Your normal workflow therefore becomes:

```text
WRITE
  ↓
Edit .qmd files
  ↓
quarto render
  ↓
CHECK
  ↓
Preview locally
  ↓
SAVE VERSION
  ↓
git add .
git commit
git push
  ↓
PUBLISH
  ↓
quarto publish gh-pages
  ↓
PUBLIC WEBSITE
```

---

## 19. The commands I use most often

After everything is configured, I only use a small number of commands regularly.

### Build

```bash
quarto render
```

### Preview

```bash
quarto preview
```

or:

```bash
python3 -m http.server 8000 --directory _site
```

### Check Git changes

```bash
git status
```

### Save changes

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Describe what I changed"
```

### Push to GitHub

```bash
git push
```

### Publish

```bash
quarto publish gh-pages
```

So although the initial setup may look complicated, the day-to-day workflow is actually quite small.

---

## 20. A few things I learned

### Keep filenames simple

Prefer:

```text
my-first-conference.qmd
```

over:

```text
My First Conference.qmd
```

I try to use:

- lowercase letters
- hyphens
- no spaces
- simple folder names

This is particularly useful because web servers are often case-sensitive.

For example:

```text
index.qmd
```

and:

```text
Index.qmd
```

may not behave as the same file after publication.

### Separate content from appearance

I keep:

```text
.qmd
```

for content and:

```text
styles.css
```

for appearance.

This makes it much easier to change the design later without rewriting the content.

### Render before publishing

I normally run:

```bash
quarto render
```

and inspect the website locally before publishing.

This catches many small problems, such as:

- Broken image paths
- Incorrect filenames
- YAML errors
- Layout problems
- Missing pages

### Commit regularly

Git becomes much more useful when commits describe meaningful changes:

```bash
git commit -m "Add conference preparation article"
```

rather than:

```bash
git commit -m "update"
```

This makes the history of the website much easier to understand later.

---

## Key concepts

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Quarto** | Converts `.qmd` content into webpages |
| **VS Code** | Editor for writing and managing files |
| **Git** | Tracks changes and versions |
| **GitHub** | Stores the Git repository online |
| **GitHub Pages** | Hosts the public website |
| **`.qmd`** | Quarto source document |
| **`.html`** | Rendered webpage |
| **`_quarto.yml`** | Website-wide configuration |
| **`styles.css`** | Custom appearance |
| **`_site/`** | Rendered website |
| **`main`** | Branch containing the source project |
| **`gh-pages`** | Branch containing the published website |

---

## Putting everything together

The whole process can be summarised as:

```text
          WRITE
            │
            ▼
        .qmd files
            │
            ▼
          QUARTO
            │
            ▼
      Rendered website
            │
            ▼
           GIT
       Track changes
            │
            ▼
          GITHUB
      Store the project
            │
            ▼
      GITHUB PAGES
            │
            ▼
       PUBLIC WEBSITE
```

You do not need to master Quarto, Git, GitHub, Markdown, CSS, and web development before building your first website.

I certainly did not.

For me, building the website itself became part of the learning process. I started with a few `.qmd` files and gradually learned how Quarto, Git, GitHub, Markdown, CSS, and GitHub Pages fit together.

The result is not only a personal website. It is also a useful way to practise **reproducible documentation, version control, scientific communication, and writing**.

And once everything is set up, publishing something new can be as simple as:

> **Write → Render → Commit → Push → Publish**
